lessons.title: Sorting and Cleaning Raw Materials: Removing Stones, Plastic, and Metal
lessons.body:
Before you can make good briquettes, you must start with clean raw materials. Whether you are using agricultural waste like maize cobs, rice husks, or sawdust, or collecting paper and cardboard, these materials often contain unwanted items that can damage your equipment or ruin your briquettes. Sorting and cleaning is the first and most important step.

Start by spreading your raw materials on a clean tarpaulin or concrete floor. Wear thick gloves to protect your hands. Pick out any stones, rocks, or pieces of metal. Stones will dull your crusher blades and can even break them. Metal pieces like nails, wire, or screws can jam your grinder and cause serious injury. Use a strong magnet to help remove small metal bitsâyou can find magnets in old speakers or buy one at a hardware store.

Plastic is another common contaminant, especially if you collect waste from markets or dumpsites. Plastic melts during burning and releases toxic fumes. It also weakens the briquette. Remove all plastic bags, wrappers, and bottles. If you are using paper, remove any plastic tape or windows from envelopes.

For fine materials like rice husks or sawdust, use a sieve or mesh screen to sift out sand, dirt, and small stones. A simple wire mesh with 5-10 mm holes works well. You can build a wooden frame and staple the mesh to it. Shake the sieve over a wheelbarrow or container. The clean material falls through, while stones and debris stay on top.

After sorting, store your clean materials in a dry, covered area to prevent recontamination. Use sacks or a covered bin. Keep them off the ground on a pallet or stones. This simple step saves you time and money by protecting your machines and ensuring consistent, high-quality briquettes.

lessons.title: Drying Methods: Sun Drying, Solar Dryers, and Simple Kilns
lessons.body:
Drying is critical because wet raw materials won't bind well and will produce smoky, crumbly briquettes. The goal is to reduce moisture content to below 15%, ideally around 10-12%. There are three main methods you can use in Africa: sun drying, solar dryers, and simple kilns.

Sun drying is the cheapest and most common method. Spread your raw materials in a thin layer (5-10 cm thick) on a black plastic sheet, concrete floor, or tarpaulin. Black absorbs heat better. Stir the material every 2-3 hours with a rake or shovel to expose fresh surfaces. In hot, dry weather (30-35Â°C), thin materials like rice husks or sawdust can dry in 1-2 days. Thicker materials like maize cobs may take 3-5 days. Cover the materials at night or if it rains. A major drawback is that you need a large flat area and good weather.

Solar dryers are more efficient and protect materials from rain and dust. A simple solar dryer is a wooden box with a transparent polythene or glass top and ventilation holes at the bottom and top. The sun heats the air inside, which rises and escapes, pulling in fresh air. You can build one using local timber and clear plastic sheets. Inside, place your materials on trays made of mesh. A solar dryer can dry materials in 1-2 days even in moderate sunshine, and it keeps them clean.

Simple kilns are used for drying and also for carbonizing materials if you want to make charcoal briquettes. A kiln is a metal drum or brick structure where you light a small fire at the bottom and let the heat and smoke dry the material above. This is faster but requires more skill and fuel. For drying only, you can use a drum with a fire underneath and a tray on top. Be careful not to burn the material. Kilns are best for large-scale operations.

Whichever method you choose, test dryness by squeezing a handful. If it crumbles and feels dry, it's ready. If it holds together like dough, it needs more drying.

lessons.title: Size Reduction: Using Manual Crushers, Grinders, and Hammermills
lessons.body:
Size reduction is the process of breaking raw materials into smaller pieces. For briquettes, you need particles that are small and uniformâusually between 2 mm and 10 mm, depending on your briquette press. Smaller particles bind better and produce denser, stronger briquettes. There are three main tools: manual crushers, grinders, and hammermills.

Manual crushers are the simplest and cheapest. They include mortar and pestle, hand-cranked grain mills, and wooden mallets. Use a mortar and pestle to crush brittle materials like charcoal, dry leaves, or small cobs. For larger quantities, a hand-cranked grinder (like those used for maize) can be adjusted to produce coarse particles. These are labor-intensive but require no fuel or electricity. They are ideal for small-scale production or when you are just starting.

Grinders (also called hammer mills or burr mills) are motorized or engine-driven. A hammer mill has rotating hammers that beat the material against a screen until it is small enough to pass through. You can buy a small hammer mill (5-10 HP) for around $300-$800. It can process 100-500 kg per hour. For agricultural residues like maize cobs, rice husks, or groundnut shells, a hammer mill is very effective. Make sure the screen size matches your desired particle size. A 5 mm screen gives you finer material; a 10 mm screen gives coarser.

Hammermills are larger and more powerful, often used in commercial operations. They can handle tough materials like wood chips, palm kernel shells, and coconut shells. They come with different screen sizes and can be powered by diesel or electric motors. A typical hammermill for briquetting costs $1,000-$3,000 and can process 500-2000 kg per hour. If you are producing more than 500 kg of briquettes per day, a hammermill is a good investment.

Whichever tool you use, always wear safety glasses, a dust mask, and gloves. Feed material slowly and evenly to avoid jamming. Keep the machine clean and sharp. After crushing, store the material in a dry place. Uniform particle size is key to consistent briquette quality.

lessons.title: Mixing Different Materials for Better Briquettes
lessons.body:
Mixing different raw materials is a smart way to improve briquette quality, reduce costs, and use what you have locally. Different materials have different properties: some burn hot, some bind well, some are cheap, and some are abundant. By blending them, you can create a briquette that is strong, burns long, and produces less smoke.

A good briquette mix usually has three components: a base material (for heat), a binder (to hold it together), and a filler (to add bulk and reduce cost). For example, charcoal dust (base) mixed with cassava starch (binder) and sawdust (filler) makes excellent charcoal briquettes. For non-carbonized briquettes, you can mix maize cobs, rice husks, and paper pulp. The ratio depends on your materials, but a common starting point is 50% base, 30% filler, and 20% binder (by dry weight).

When mixing, aim for a uniform blend. Use a shovel or hoe to turn the pile at least three times. For small batches, mix in a wheelbarrow or on a clean tarpaulin. For larger batches, a cement mixer or a simple drum mixer works well. Add water gradually while mixing until the mixture holds together when squeezed but doesn't drip. The ideal moisture for pressing is 15-25% depending on your press.

Test different ratios. Make a small batch (e.g., 5 kg) and press a few briquettes. Let them dry and then test how they burn. Adjust the mix: if they crumble, add more binder; if they burn too fast, add more dense material like charcoal fines; if they smoke too much, reduce the amount of green or wet materials. Keep records of what works. Local materials like cassava peels, banana peels, and coconut shells can also be dried and ground to add binding or heat value.

Remember, consistency is key. Once you find a mix that works, stick to it and measure your ingredients by weight or volume. This ensures every batch of briquettes performs the same. Mixing is not just about combining materialsâit's about creating a product that meets your customers' needs.

lessons.title: Adding Binders: Cassava Starch, Clay, and Other Local Options
lessons.body:
Binders are the glue that holds briquettes together. Without a good binder, your briquettes will crumble and fall apart. The binder helps particles stick together under pressure and keeps the briquette intact after drying. There are many local binder options in Africa, and the best one depends on your raw materials and what is available.

Cassava starch is one of the best binders. It is cheap, widely available, and works well. To make cassava starch binder, peel and wash fresh cassava tubers, then grate or blend them. Mix the grated cassava with water (about 1 part cassava to 3 parts water) and stir. You can also use cassava flour: mix 1 kg of flour with 10 liters of water and heat gently until it forms a thick paste. This paste is then mixed with your raw materials. Use about 5-10% binder by weight of dry materials. For example, for 10 kg of dry material, use 0.5-1 kg of cassava starch. Cassava binder gives strong briquettes but can attract insects if not dried properly.

Clay is another common binder. Use fine clay soil, not sandy soil. Dry the clay, crush it, and mix with water to form a slurry. Add the slurry to your raw materials. Clay is very cheap and improves the briquette's ability to hold together during burning. However, clay adds ash and reduces heat value. Use only 5-15% clay by weight. Too much clay makes the briquette burn poorly.

Other local binders include: wheat flour (works like cassava but more expensive), rice starch (from broken rice or rice water), okra mucilage (from boiled okra), and even cow dung (for non-food use, but it smells). You can also use waste paper pulp as a binderâsoak waste paper in water for 24 hours, then blend it into a pulp. Paper pulp is excellent for binding and is free if you collect waste paper.

To use any binder, mix it thoroughly with your dry materials before adding water. The binder should be evenly distributed. Then add water until the mixture reaches the right consistency. Test by squeezing a handful: it should hold together without dripping. Let the briquettes dry completely before use. With the right binder, your briquettes will be strong, durable, and easy to handle.

lessons.title: Achieving the Right Moisture Level for Pressing
lessons.body:
Moisture level is the most critical factor in briquette pressing. If the mixture is too dry, the briquettes will crumble and not hold together. If it's too wet, the briquettes will be soft, take too long to dry, and may grow mold. The ideal moisture content for pressing is usually between 15% and 25%, depending on your press type and raw materials. For manual presses, aim for 20-25%; for motorized presses, 15-20% is better.

How do you know if you have the right moisture? The squeeze test is the simplest method. Take a handful of the mixed material and squeeze it tightly in your fist. Open your hand. The material should form a ball that holds its shape but does not drip water. If it drips, it's too wetâadd more dry material and mix. If it crumbles and falls apart, it's too dryâadd a little water and mix again. Repeat until you get a firm ball that doesn't stick to your hand.

For more accuracy, you can use a moisture meter. These are available at agricultural supply stores or online for $20-$50. A simple moisture meter has two prongs that you stick into the material. It gives a reading in percentage. If you don't have a meter, you can do a rough test by weighing a sample before and after drying. Weigh 100 g of your mixture, dry it in an oven or under the sun until completely dry, then weigh again. The weight loss is the moisture. For example, if it weighs 80 g after drying, the moisture was 20%.

Adjusting moisture: If your mixture is too wet, spread it out on a tarpaulin in the sun for 1-2 hours, stirring occasionally. Or add more dry raw material. If it's too dry, add water gradually using a watering can or spray bottle, mixing continuously. Never dump water all at onceâyou might overshoot. Always mix thoroughly after each addition.

Once you have the right moisture, press your briquettes immediately. Don't let the mixture sit for too long, as it can dry out or ferment. Pressed briquettes should be placed in a shaded, ventilated area to dry slowly. Rapid drying in direct sun can cause cracks. With practice, you will develop a feel for the right moisture, and your briquettes will be consistently strong and burn well.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Preparing Raw Materials for Briquetting

In briquette and pellet production, raw material preparation accounts for up to 60% of total production cost and determines whether your final product burns cleanly, holds together, and sells at a profit. Across Africa â from cassava peels in Nigeria to rice husks in Tanzania, maize cobs in Kenya, and sawdust in Ghana â the difference between a briquette business that thrives and one that fails often comes down to how well you sort, dry, grind, mix, bind, and moisture-balance your feedstock before pressing.

This practical reference distils the six preparation stages into a business-first workflow you can apply on any scale: from a 50 kg/day manual operation to a 2-tonne/day semi-industrial line.

1. Sorting and Cleaning Raw Materials: Removing Stones, Plastic, and Metal

Contamination is the number-one cause of equipment failure and product rejection. Stones and metal shatter hammers and dies; plastic melts into the binder matrix and produces toxic fumes when the briquette burns; sand and grit reduce calorific value and increase ash content.

Practical sorting sequence for African feedstock:

  • Visual pick: Remove plastic bags, nylon, cloth, and large stones by hand on a sorting table or tarpaulin.
  • Magnetic separation: A simple permanent magnet (or magnetic pulley) over the conveyor catches nails, wire, and scrap metal.
  • Screening: A 10â20 mm mesh screen removes sand, soil, and fines before drying.
  • Density separation: For mixed municipal or market waste, a simple water float-sink or air classifier separates heavy inerts.
  • Quality gate: Reject any batch with visible plastic â one contaminated tonne can ruin a week of production.

2. Drying Methods: Sun Drying, Solar Dryers, and Simple Kilns

Moisture is the enemy of briquetting. Wet feedstock clogs hammermills, produces steam explosions in the press, and yields weak, mould-prone briquettes. Target feedstock moisture before grinding is typically 10â15%; before pressing, 8â12% depending on binder and press type.

Three drying options, ranked by cost and reliability:

Table 1: Comparison of Drying Methods for Briquette Feedstock in Africa
Method Typical Drying Time Capital Cost (USD) Best For Efficiency
Open sun drying (tarpaulin/concrete) 3â7 days 0â200 Small-scale, dry-season production Low; weather-dependent
Solar dryer (greenhouse/box type) 1â3 days 300â2,500 Year-round SME production Medium-high; 40â70% faster than sun
Simple kiln / biomass dryer 4â12 hours 1,500â8,000 Industrial scale, wet season, high volume High; fuel or waste-heat driven

Source: Adapted from FAO (2017), "Simple Technologies for Charcoal Making" and SNV/Kenya (2019), "Briquette Business Models in East Africa."

3. Size Reduction: Using Manual Crushers, Grinders, and Hammermills

Particle size controls briquette density, durability, and burn rate. The general rule: finer particles â denser, stronger briquettes, but finer grinding costs more energy. Target particle size:

  • Manual press briquettes: 5â10 mm
  • Hydraulic/screw extruder: 3â5 mm
  • Pellet mill: 3â6 mm
Table 2: Size Reduction Equipment Selection Guide
Equipment Throughput Power Cost (USD) Particle Size Output
Manual crusher / mortar 20â100 kg/hr Human 50â300 10â20 mm
Diesel/electric grinder 200â800 kg/hr 5â15 kW 800â3,500 3â8 mm
Hammermill 500â3,000 kg/hr 11â45 kW 2,500â12,000 2â6 mm

Source: Adapted from FAO (1990), "Agricultural Engineering in Development: Equipment for Processing" and GIZ (2020), "Biomass Briquetting Technology and Practices."

4. Mixing Different Materials for Better Briquettes

Single-feedstock briquettes are rarely optimal. Blending improves calorific value, combustion, and mechanical strength. Proven African blends:

  • Rice husk (60%) + sawdust (40%) â high silica husk needs sawdust's lignin to bind.
  • Maize cob (50%) + cassava peel (30%) + sawdust (20%) â balanced density and burn time.
  • Charcoal fines (70%) + clay (20%) + starch (10%) â classic cookstove briquette.
  • Groundnut shell (50%) + palm kernel shell (50%) â high energy, good for industrial use.

Mix in a horizontal mixer, concrete mixer, or even on a clean concrete floor with shovels for small batches. Aim for homogeneity within 5% â visible colour streaks mean poor mixing.

5. Adding Binders: Cassava Starch, Clay, and Other Local Options

Binders hold particles together and determine briquette durability. Local, low-cost options dominate African production:

  • Cassava starch (5â10% dry weight): Best all-round binder. Gelatinise by cooking in hot water before mixing. Cost: low where cassava is grown.
  • Clay / bentonite (10â20%): Cheap, widely available, but increases ash and reduces calorific value. Use sparingly.
  • Molasses (5â15%): Excellent binding and adds energy; can attract insects if briquettes are stored damp.
  • Waste paper pulp (5â10%): Free in urban areas; good for charcoal briquettes.
  • Palm oil mill effluent (POME) sludge: Emerging binder in West Africa; needs drying.
â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Binder and Dust Hazards

Biomass dust is explosive and carcinogenic. Always wear an N95 dust mask, safety goggles, and gloves when grinding, mixing, and handling dry feedstock. Never operate a hammermill in an enclosed space without forced ventilation â dust explosions have killed operators across Africa. When cooking cassava starch binder, use heat-resistant gloves to avoid scalds. Store molasses and starch binders away from pesticides and fuel to prevent cross-contamination of the final briquette. Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher within 5 metres of all grinding and mixing equipment.

6. Achieving the Right Moisture Level for Pressing

Moisture is the single most controllable variable in briquette quality. Too wet â weak, mouldy briquettes, press clogging, steam explosions. Too dry â crumbly briquettes that fail to bind.

Target moisture before pressing:

  • Manual / low-pressure press: 12â18%
  • Hydraulic press: 8â12%
  • Screw extruder: 6â10%
  • Pellet mill: 10â15%

Low-cost moisture test (the "squeeze test"): Take a handful of mixed feedstock, squeeze firmly. If it holds shape without dripping water and crumbles when poked, moisture is close to target. For accuracy, use a moisture meter (USD 30â150) â a worthwhile investment for any commercial operation.

If too wet: spread on drying bed for 2â6 hours, or add dry feedstock to the mix. If too dry: spray water evenly while mixing â never dump water in one spot.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Sort feedstock on a clean tarpaulin â remove all plastic, metal, and stones before any processing.
  2. â Run a magnet over the feedstock to catch nails and wire.
  3. â Screen out sand and soil with a 10â20 mm mesh.
  4. â Dry feedstock to 10â15% moisture before grinding; test with a moisture meter or squeeze test.
  5. â Grind to 3â6 mm for most press types; check by sieving a sample.
  6. â Blend 2â3 feedstocks for better density, burn time, and strength.
  7. â Add binder (5â10% cassava starch is the safest default) and mix until uniform.
  8. â Re-check moisture (8â12% for pressing) and adjust before feeding the press.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Simple Technologies for Charcoal Making (full technical manual, free download).
  • GIZ â Biomass Briquetting Technology and Practices (practical SME guide).
  • U.S. DOE Bioenergy â Biomass Feedstock Library (moisture and composition data).
  • Africa Clean Energy â Clean Cooking Alliance Resources (regional market and standards).
  • IRENA â Bioenergy Publications (policy, finance, and technology reports).

Business takeaway: A briquette business that controls raw material preparation â sorting, drying, grinding, mixing, binding, and moisture â produces a consistent product that supermarkets, schools, restaurants, and industries will re-order. Inconsistent quality kills repeat sales faster than any competitor. Treat preparation as your production line's foundation, and your margins will follow.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove stones from raw materials before briquetting?
options: A) Stones make the briquettes burn hotter
B) Stones can damage crusher blades and equipment
C) Stones add useful minerals to the briquettes
D) Stones help bind the materials together
quiz.explanation: Stones can dull or break crusher blades and cause equipment damage.

quiz.q: Which tool can help you remove small metal pieces from raw materials?
quiz.explanation: A magnet attracts and removes small metal bits like nails and wire.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of leaving plastic in raw materials?
options: A) It makes the briquettes too hard
B) It releases toxic fumes when burned
C) It increases the heat value
D) It helps the briquettes dry faster
quiz.explanation: Plastic melts and releases toxic fumes when burned, which is harmful.

quiz.q: What size mesh screen is recommended for sifting out sand and small stones?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 mm mesh is effective for sifting out sand and small stones while letting fine material through.

quiz.q: After sorting, how should clean raw materials be stored?
options: A) In an open pile on the ground
B) In a dry, covered area off the ground
C) In a wet area to keep them from drying
quiz.explanation: Storing in a dry, covered area off the ground prevents recontamination and moisture absorption.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for raw materials before pressing briquettes?
quiz.explanation: The ideal moisture for pressing is typically 15-25%, depending on the press and material.

quiz.q: Which drying method is the cheapest and most common in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sun drying is the cheapest and most widely used method due to abundant sunlight.

quiz.q: How thick should you spread materials for sun drying?
quiz.explanation: A thin layer of 5-10 cm allows for faster and more even drying.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a solar dryer over sun drying?
options: A) It is cheaper to build
B) It protects materials from rain and dust
D) It dries materials faster than any other method
quiz.explanation: Solar dryers protect materials from rain, dust, and pests while drying.

quiz.q: What is a simple kiln used for in briquette production?
quiz.explanation: Simple kilns can be used for both drying and carbonizing materials.

quiz.q: What is the recommended particle size range for briquette raw materials?
quiz.explanation: Particles between 2 mm and 10 mm are ideal for good binding and dense briquettes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a manual size reduction tool?
quiz.explanation: A mortar and pestle is a simple manual tool for crushing materials.

quiz.q: What is the typical processing capacity of a small hammer mill (5-10 HP)?
quiz.explanation: A small hammer mill can process about 100-500 kg per hour.

quiz.q: Why is uniform particle size important for briquettes?
options: A) It makes briquettes burn faster
B) It ensures better binding and stronger briquettes
C) It reduces the need for a binder
D) It makes the briquettes lighter
quiz.explanation: Uniform particles bind better, producing denser and stronger briquettes.

quiz.q: What safety gear should you wear when operating a hammermill?
options: B) Safety glasses, dust mask, and gloves
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses, dust mask, and gloves protect against flying particles and dust.

quiz.q: What is a common ratio for a good briquette mix?
quiz.explanation: A typical starting ratio is 50% base, 30% filler, and 20% binder by dry weight.

quiz.q: How many times should you turn a pile when mixing briquette materials?
quiz.explanation: Turning the pile at least three times ensures a uniform blend.

quiz.q: What should you do if your briquette mixture crumbles after drying?
quiz.explanation: Crumbling indicates insufficient binder; adding more binder improves cohesion.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of your briquette mix ratios?
options: B) To ensure consistency and repeatability
C) To reduce the cost of materials
quiz.explanation: Records help you replicate successful mixes and maintain consistent quality.

quiz.q: Which of these is a local binder commonly used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cassava starch is a cheap, effective, and widely available local binder.

quiz.q: How much cassava starch binder should you use by weight of dry materials?
quiz.explanation: Use about 5-10% cassava starch by weight of dry materials for good binding.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of using clay as a binder?
options: B) It adds ash and reduces heat value
C) It is not available locally
D) It makes briquettes burn too fast
quiz.explanation: Clay adds ash and lowers the heat value of briquettes, so use it sparingly.

quiz.q: Which waste material can be soaked and blended to make a free binder?
quiz.explanation: Waste paper soaked and blended into pulp makes an excellent free binder.

quiz.q: What is the squeeze test used for?
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test helps determine if the mixture has the right moisture for pressing.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for a manual briquette press?
quiz.explanation: Manual presses typically require a higher moisture content of 20-25%.

quiz.q: If a handful of mixture drips water when squeezed, what should you do?
options: B) Add more dry material and mix
D) Let it sit for an hour
quiz.explanation: Dripping means too wet; add dry material to absorb excess moisture.

quiz.q: How can you roughly measure moisture content without a meter?
options: B) By weighing a sample before and after drying
quiz.explanation: Weighing before and after drying gives the moisture percentage by weight loss.

quiz.q: What should you do if your mixture is too dry?
options: A) Add water gradually while mixing
D) Let it sit in the sun
quiz.explanation: Add water gradually and mix thoroughly to reach the right moisture.

quiz.q: Why should pressed briquettes be dried in a shaded, ventilated area?
options: A) To make them dry faster
B) To prevent cracks from rapid drying
quiz.explanation: Slow drying in shade prevents cracks and uneven drying.

quiz.q: What is the consequence of pressing briquettes with too much moisture?
options: B) They are soft, take long to dry, and may grow mold
quiz.explanation: Excess moisture leads to soft briquettes, long drying times, and mold growth.
